This paper presents corollaries stemming from Korovkin theorems in order-preserving contexts, specifically involving weakly nonlinear operators. It reformulates the corollaries in terms of operators, highlighting their implications for translating Korovkin theorems into for operators. Building upon the reformulation, the paper introduces sufficient and necessary conditions for a class of nonlinear and monotonic operators to satisfy the L-theorem. Notably, the paper demonstrates the applicability of the derived conditions in determining whether a weakly nonlinear and monotonic operator class adheres to the L-theorem. A comparative analysis with established results is also provided to underscore the paper's novel contributions.

A graph is classified as pancyclic if it contains cycles of every possible length from 3 to n, where n represents the graph's size. Researchers in 1985, specifically Dorfling, established a condition that guarantees a graph to be pancyclic based on its Hamiltonian strength. We have later refined and generalized this result, developing more comprehensive conditions that not only determine if a graph contains all possible cycles but also ensure it has the highest level of cycle existence. We have explored the connection between the highest label in a graph's cycle decomposition and the highest label in its Hamiltonian cycle decomposition, ultimately establishing conditions that ensure the graph contains all possible cycles. We have shown that these conditions depend on the graph's Hamiltonian strength and other topological properties, such as its minimum degree and its minimum degree's maximum value plus one. We have also demonstrated that these conditions are the best possible when the graph's size is 3k+2, where k represents an integer.

The two-proton correlation function, derived from non-relativistic quantum mechanical scattering theory, can be explained through the interference of two protons related to their shared source characteristics, specifically their size and momentum distribution variance. When applying a correlation function model based on proton movement patterns in heavy-ion collisions at the LHC and RHIC energies, researchers have observed a relationship between the protons' interaction strength, referred to as optical hadron potential, and momentum. Studies involving proton-proton collisions from Au+Au and isobar interactions at the same energy level revealed that the protons' interaction strength remains consistent regardless of the heavy-ion species involved.

To implement the non-invasive, data-driven adaptive spectral Koopman approach, numerous time series are required in the past, future, and present states, making it difficult to apply to systems like human brain fMRI data, which are limited in size and highly noisy. To address this challenge, we introduce a strategy to reduce the data requirements and improve signal quality by driving the spectral Koopman analysis with a sparsity constraint in the l0-norm, which allows for more efficient utilization of limited data and better detection of dominant patterns in systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach using a 2x2 linear Koopman operator and the human brain fMRI data, showing that it can accurately recover the true Koopman operator with limited data and efficiently analyze the complex fMRI data.

A new approach, known as the outside complicated scaling (OCS) method, has been created to study how atoms and molecules react to strong direct current electric fields. This method utilizes the logarithmic of distance outside a computed low-field model wavefunction to predict the energy associated with these systems in an external electric field of any strength. Comparing this new method to established methods such as adiabatic ionization and atomic or molecular tunneling ionization shows that the outside OCS method offers a more accurate measurement, particularly at the extremes of very strong or very weak external electric fields where other methods fail or become unreliable.

The convergence of the Sinkhorn method is typically assumed under the presence of a unique solution to the Schrödinger system. Contrary to established results, we challenge this finding by demonstrating that a unique solution to the problem can arise without the issue of degeneracy. Moreover, we establish a new approach for analyzing the convergence of the Sinkhorn method even when there is no solution to this system, effectively assuming degenerated behaviour on a set of measure zero. We achieve this by modifying the basic KK-box algorithm and show that it remains equivalent to a continuous dynamics. The mathematical foundation of our proof involves the theory of scalar viscosities and proves global convergence of the modified algorithm to the barycentric projection of the two process' distributions. The implications of our findings significantly expand upon the existing body of literature.

Measurements of the production cross-section for $t\text{-}\bar{t}$ are conducted at the LHC at a collision energy of 5.02 TeV and recorded by the ATLAS detector. The analysis utilizes data containing 19.6 inverse femtobarns of integrated luminosity, which corresponds to collisions in proton. The $t\text{-}\bar{t}$ events are divided into three categories based on their composition: two with at least one or two leptons, and one with no leptons present. Cross-section measurements are calculated for each group and combined to yield a single value. The results indicate that the $t\text{-}\bar{t}$ cross-section is consistent with the predictions made by next-to-leading order QCD calculations at approximately 1% accuracy for a combined value and with an uncertainty of 3% when considering just the leptonic category. The predicted value for the next-to-next-to-leading order QCD calculations is exceeded by approximately three standard deviations for the full measurement.

A central linkage in a network connects its communities and affects their characteristics. Central linkages can induce a localized structure within a network, and a mean field approach has been developed to examine the localization behavior in networks with communities and a central hub. The model we propose uses simple assumptions, and it can accurately describe the localization behavior and phase transition in central linked systems using central links and degree distributions that follow power laws. We also found that network size and distribution exponents impact the appearance of a localized phase in networks with communities and central hubs.

This paper demonstrates that Bessel-Janowski functions form a key subset within the broader class of Janowski functions. Further, it reveals specific characteristics of functions belonging to the Bessel-Janowski category, including the maximum possible values for coefficients and degree of such functions along with explicit formulas for all coefficients of a particular sub-group known as Bessel functions of the first kind with negative indices.

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has led to significant alterations in people's daily routines and social behaviors, yet researchers struggle to account for these changes in the dynamics of urban areas.  In this study, we introduce modified versions of human mobility data that take into consideration factors such as pandemic-related restrictions and individual risk behaviors.  By analyzing this revised data, we discover that the pandemic has contributed to an increase in inequality among urban neighborhoods, particularly during the period from March 2020 to July 2020, with some specific patterns such as reduced movement within working districts and heightened travel to suburban areas.  Furthermore, we investigate how different pandemic-related measures and personal risk behaviors have influenced urban movement patterns and found that stricter pandemic-related restrictions tend to reduce disparity, whereas individual risk behaviors tend to increase disparity.  In light of these findings, we suggest potential public health and urban planning interventions aimed at minimizing neighborhood inequality.

This research delves into novel field-separated preconditioners for multiphase flow within porous media, particularly media with irregular structures. These preconditioners utilize field-separated approximations of the mobility matrix to expedite the convergence of nonlinear solutions when simulating time-dependent two-phase flow. The study focuses solely on nonlinear convergence, disregarding any possible disadvantages arising from grid refinement. The development of these preconditioners draws from the field-separated multicomponent pressure-velocity-temperature approach originally introduced by Dullien. The research compares the performance of different preconditioners, incorporating three distinct methods of calculating relative permeability and relative solubility, namely the JAG, the LOG, and the Geometric mean methods. The findings indicate that while the LOG mean method is the most suitable for general applications, higher concentrations of a phase may benefit from the use of the geometric mean method, and highly heterogeneous media can be better handled with the JAG method. Furthermore, it's observed that when employing a LOG mean method, higher values of water saturation lead to faster convergence, and significant improvements in convergence rates can be achieved by using these preconditioners, particularly in highly heterogeneous and angled grids where they facilitate the use of larger time steps and reduce computational costs.

We propose a design for a one-way optical enclosure utilizing a single flat gain medium and individual filters that absorb the incoming light. Our configuration ensures that the trap can be opened from one side only and effectively traps both traveling and stationary chemical waves within its boundaries, allowing minimal leakage of information or energy in the process.

Our research focuses on the connection between the Witten Liouville Conformal Field Theory and the Gopakumar Vafa Kontsevich's Riemann Surface Loop Space (KRC), which is derived from the 2D JT Gravity path integral. The 2D JT Gravity path integral is essentially a sum over all possible 2D metrics with specific boundary conditions and punctures, which can be translated into a sum over modular data and conformal blocks, represented by Liouville CFT correlation functions. The Witten Liouville Conformal Field Theory has a well-defined quantization framework through the Fock Space/Qi-Fuchs-Niyamiyama (QFN) free boson field theory, represented by the KRC in a matrix framework. This perspective allows us to relate JT Gravity to Random Matrix Theory, and demonstrate its equivalence to matrix models with prescribed spectral data. Furthermore, we establish a connection between asymptotic spectral data and asymptotic spectral density through the use of Riemann surfaces and spectral curves, which are represented by the Fuchsian equations and the spectral measure of the corresponding operator.

A new set of homogeneous space warp drive solutions, referred to as "fluid warp drives," has been identified, derived from the Einstein equations. These solutions, particularly those that are static and spherically symmetric, include the de Sitter solution and extend to the presence of a cosmological constant. Notably, the metric for these solutions, applicable to both scenarios, reveals a specific relationship between the shape function and the properties of the fluid, which depends on the cosmological constant. Further analysis has yielded a family of non-static, non-homogeneous space warp drive solutions, and it's observed that conditions similar to those of anti-gravity are required for their feasibility.

New York City's Department of Transportation is collaborating with its partners 
to develop the GUIDES platform, an internet-based service that integrates 
comprehensive data on New York City's metropolitan infrastructure.  This 
integrated dataset is organized into distinct resolution tiers to accommodate 
various user needs and perspectives, spanning diverse infomediary levels.  By 
employing a unified data framework, GUIDES enables seamless data fusion across 
these tiers to support in-depth infrastructure analysis.  By breaking down and 
identifying the distinct data components within each resolution tier, GUIDES 
facilitates a thorough deconstruction of the metropolitan region.  By leveraging 
these granular building blocks, users can perform detailed, step-by-step analyses 
of the region's infrastructure.  Furthermore, GUIDES incorporates various 
infrastructure data sources from diverse resolution tiers to provide a holistic 
and up-to-date picture of New York City's metropolitan infrastructure.

The dynamics of thermal equilibrium establishment and specific heat capacity of Larmor-minimized spherical ions have been investigated. A spin decay analysis provided valuable insights into the Pecora-Taylor high-temperature regime of phonon-induced collisions, specifically how the lattice size and 2D geometry influence these processes. Our findings confirm that a simplified model of thermal motion is highly effective in explaining observed temperature dependencies and indicate that the lattice reaches a local thermal equilibrium on a timescale of tens of milliseconds. By adjusting parameters such as perturbation magnitude and detection intervals, we were able to study uniformly anisotropic hard-sphere dynamics under conditions far from thermal equilibrium. This research further reveals that the spin decay is primarily governed by the uniform anisotropic hard-sphere model. Our work challenges previous estimates of specific heat and energy relaxation times, and reveals a direct relationship between detected contact ion distributions and motion states. These findings are of significant value for optimizing occupancy distributions to study various low-temperature phenomena.

The electrochemical effect is a critical factor in explaining the significantly enhanced Raman signals that can be observed in TERS experiments. However, there have been various proposed theories to explain this phenomenon, and there is still no universally accepted explanation. A novel approach based on time-dependent density functional theory has been proposed to clarify this issue by considering the effects of both chemistry and electric fields. In this study, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of qEDFT in predicting the significantly enhanced Raman cross-section in TERS experiments, particularly when there is a strong electrochemical effect present, such as the adsorption of molecules on a metal surface. The results of our simulations show excellent agreement with existing experimental data and highlight the importance of electrochemical effects in TERS.

We investigated the Milky Way analog galaxy, NGC 4631, to examine whether nearby spiral galaxies exhibit unique microwave radiation. Utilizing the Sardinia Radio Telescope, we conducted a thorough search for this radiation across a wide area of the galaxy's disk and disk halo at a resolution of approximately 10 km/s and a sensitivity of about 3 microJy/beam. Our findings show no microwave bubble signatures within about 10 kiloparsecs of the galaxy's center or beyond 8 kiloparsecs in its halo. Moreover, we observed no sign of microwave radiation originating from the galaxy's wind or a radio halo at a significantly lower frequency. Nonetheless, we successfully detected synchrotron emission from the galaxy's jet-like features and a nearby shell, both of which were observed with an estimated flux of approximately 100 mJy. Our study also revealed the presence of microwave emission from a galactic outflow located within about 3 kiloparsecs of the galaxy's center and extending at least 5 kiloparsecs beyond the galaxy's center. This discovery provides the first observational evidence of a galactic wind's ability to generate magnetohydrodynamic turbulence within the outer regions of a galaxy's hot interstellar medium. This work emphasizes the need for further research into the magnetohydrodynamic turbulence in galactic winds and the exploration of similar emission in a broader range of galaxy samples.

Thermal entropy alteration can be observed in molecules, which exhibits a significant magnitude.  Traditionally, this phenomenon was attributed to a substantial change in intermolecular forces, which is contrary to expectations.  In contrast, we observed a substantial thermal entropy alteration in ammonium sulfate, which is also a molecular substance with substantial entropy alteration of 13.1 J/mol K.  However, we discovered that this phenomenon arises not from a change in lattice forces but from the substantial change in molecular entropy.  Moreover, we found that this thermal entropy alteration is a general phenomenon occurring across various substance types, which is present in both liquids and solids, as well as ferroelectrics and non-ferroelectrics, and is linked to the molecular reorientation phenomenon.  Additionally, it is proposed that thermal entropy alteration is a general property of molecules, which can potentially be used to predict a molecule's capability to be used in molecular materials for calorics and calorimetry applications.

In reinforcement learning (RL), agents learn to maximize their expected future rewards.  However, when an actual reward is received that differs from their expectations, the agent must adjust their reward estimations.  This process involves an update rate known as the learning rate. Traditionally, scientists have focused on the simplest form of RL where a fixed learning rate is used for all rewards.  However, in reality, it is likely that different rewards are processed by separate learning systems with varying update rates.  When multiple systems are at play, they can interact in different ways.  One study investigated how different combinations of RL systems with varying update rates are associated with brain activity, specifically in response to unexpected rewards.  Researchers used advanced machine learning techniques to create complex RL models that could accurately predict which rewards people would choose in various scenarios.  By analyzing data from 200 participants, they identified that when people use a RL system with an intermediate update rate, it is associated with increased activity in a part of the brain called the midbrain.  In contrast, using a system with a lower update rate is associated with midbrain activity related to the anticipation of rewards, while using a system with a higher update rate is associated with midbrain activity related to prediction errors.  Ultimately, they found that using a system with a lower update rate is associated with activity in the midbrain related to the expectation of rewards, while using a system with a higher update rate is associated with activity in the midbrain related

A proposed approach utilizing complexified $E_8$ root structure, as well as its related even lattices, is explored in quantum theory. Notably, sequential sequences in this root structure exhibit characteristics similar to contextually ordered triples in quantum mechanics. By comparing the count of triples in a specific ordered sequence to those in a conventional measurement system, the Konig distance can be calculated to measure entropy in quantum states. Quantum entanglement and contextuality are also represented within complexified $E_8$ root structure, where tensored vectors in a complex space and associated measurements correspond to specific planes within this structure.

This study investigates the task of rapidly determining if a query curve is close to a curve within a dataset, but focuses on a more constrained problem where the curve must be close to at least one curve in the dataset. The algorithm must find a curve from the dataset that is close to the query, but it can fail to find a match if the query curve is close to multiple curves, but no single curve is close to the query. The authors propose a new algorithm to solve this problem for curves of different lengths, but it relies on a parameter k that must be greater than the maximum possible number of times the query curve can intersect with a curve from the dataset that is close to the query. Real-world problems of assessing error mitigation (EM) techniques for noisy quantum computers are hindered by the limited resources, as they often require multiple experimental runs to gather the necessary information. We propose a resource-efficient iterative Bayesian approach that can determine the various error mitigation methods' error rates, gate error mitigation, and noiseless simulation (NS) accuracies, given the noisy quantum circuit's parameters. Our approach can adapt to different scenarios by specifying certain parameters. We conducted a noise characterization experiment on the IBM quantum processor using our approach, successfully achieving a 10x reduction in computation time while accurately predicting results. Furthermore, our approach can be extended to handle circuits with multiple qubits, and demonstrates consistent results with state-of-the-art methods in quantum computing.

A cutting-edge and scalable approach to robotics employs a decentralized, low-latency architecture called Collective Autonomy (CA), where multiple robots collaborate in unison. The CA framework is designed to handle tight synchronization between robots, allowing it to facilitate applications such as cooperative driving, robotics, and autonomous vehicles. The framework's key features include CA agents, which represent individual robots, and CA channels, which serve as communication pathways. The CA architecture is built upon the CA framework, which is low-level, real-time, and distributed. The framework is designed to be modular and easily combined with other frameworks, allowing it to facilitate applications that require collective behavior. The framework's design is transparent and does not interfere with other frameworks, allowing it to facilitate applications that require tight synchronization between multiple robots.

Existing map representations excel in conveying comprehensive global context, but often fall short in accurately depicting unfamiliar environments due to an excessive amount of information. To strike a balance between completeness and efficiency, we propose HiTMap, an innovative hierarchical topological map format consisting of two key components: a broad overview map capturing overall context, and a detailed local refinement map enhancing representational quality locally. The compact, topological nature of HiTMap enables efficient learning and rapid navigation within environments, further bolstered by the adoption of order-aware short sequence models to preserve critical inter-spatial relationships. The effectiveness of HiTMap is demonstrated through its superior performance in navigating environments, surpassing state-of-the-art methods in both simulated and real-world settings.

In recent years, various methods have been developed to generate inter-group complementary code sets using multivariable functions, specifically the sign-inverted Hadamard matrix and a finite field permutation. Although effective in producing sets with zero inter-group cross-correlation properties, these techniques result in suboptimal designs in terms of inter-group code set size and cross-correlation value. On the other hand, a novel development, known as the multivariable function-generated complementary code, has shown great potential in achieving large cross-correlation values while maintaining low peak-to-average power ratio. However, directly applying this new code set results in non-zero inter-group cross-correlation values, and a specific instance of the set, derived from a quadratic function, fails to meet the requirements for inter-group code sets. In order to address this issue, a novel set of inter-group complementary codes is proposed by combining a finite field linear transformation with a quadratic function. The size of the proposed code set remains identical to that of the multivariable function-generated complementary code set, and a specific instance of the set has been designed with an average cross-correlation value significantly lower than any other design to date for a code set of length 64 with 32 members. Additionally, a two-dimensional zero-sum cross-correlation code set can also be constructed through an extension of a multivariable function-generated complementary code set.

Achieving high-quality and accurate reconstructions of multiple energy CT scans is a complex challenge due to limited data and varying x-ray source noise levels, which necessitate multiple energy acquisitions and can lead to increased data dimensions. To address this issue, a novel reconstruction approach is developed, involving multiple materials and a single detector receiving input from a multi-energy CT system. This method reconstructs multiple images corresponding to each material using various x-ray energy levels while maintaining consistency with the data. To enhance the quality of the reconstructions, a joint variational model incorporating a non-convex sparsity prior is formulated and adapted for a multi-channel data set through a non-convex polyenergetic reconstruction equation. Experimental validation of the approach demonstrates its effectiveness, particularly when data is noisy, with results showing improved reconstructions compared to standard compressed sensing techniques.

A two-band model, which includes a single conduction band and a second band, is used to study the influence of a non-relativistic electron outflow on two-dimensional and one-dimensional gap-plasmons in metal nanogaps formed by two closely spaced slabs separated by a very small distance. Calculations based on the random phase approximation reveal that a wide range of modes becomes unstable once the filling ratio of the conduction band drops below a certain threshold. This occurs because of the band structure, which significantly contributes to the outflow's impact. Additionally, incorporating a finite range in the long-wave limit reveals a $-r_s$ scaling in the corrected dielectric function, which significantly suppresses the outflow's impact. Furthermore, nonlocality, which becomes increasingly significant at lower resolutions, plays a crucial role in stabilizing modes within a very small $r_s$ range.

To tackle the issue of context-dependent named entity recognition, where individual tokens may have multiple potential meanings, we propose an extension to existing named entity recognition systems. Our approach involves a classification model that assesses the likelihood of important term parts contributing to an entity's classification and at what point they are being considered. This enables the recovery of non-obvious term tokens that significantly contribute to an entity's classification, even if they are not present in traditional models. Our experiments on both artificial and real-world datasets reveal that the point of a token's contribution to an entity's classification is a stable and learnable feature. Notably, the additional token tokens identified by our model on top of those already identified by a baseline model exhibit a strong correlation with human judgment and a considerable improvement in entity recognition accuracy when combined.

To enhance interaction with linear data, we extend its structure to 2D or 3D forms to create richer contexts and then incorporate richer interactions on these higher-dimensional sequences. We incorporate two main interactions: 1) navigating and exploring data across multiple dimensions, and 2) navigating and exploring this data in both time and space on 2D or 3D paths, respectively. Our proposed interfaces demonstrate their utility through several examples showcasing their effectiveness.

Digital health records are increasingly being utilized to make vital decisions in medical settings, supplementing or even replacing traditional expert opinions. However, a significant challenge remains in extracting meaningful information from unstructured medical texts. Current methods that employ large language models often lack diversity and do not effectively capture the nuances required for accurate medical decision-making. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel approach that uses graph-based similarity and similarity diversity to enhance medical record analysis. Our proposed pipeline involves constructing similarity graphs to explore similarity diversity, which serves as a crucial component in developing a diverse similarity graph neural network for medical record classification. By training this network to generate similarity diversity-oriented representations, our approach achieves superior performance and more reliable medical decision-making. Our solution has been successfully tested on two large-scale medical datasets, including the AMI and MIMIC-III datasets, with impressive results demonstrating state-of-the-art performance and significant improvements over existing methods.

This study explores the impact of a polar solvent on the electrostatic behavior of a polymeric interface within an electrolyte solution, using advanced computer simulations. A dielectric solvent background and varying interface thickness are considered. By applying a complex mathematical technique and molecular dynamics simulations that account for a hybrid solvent model, this study investigates the effect of solvent polarization on the interface's electric double layer. For comparison, we utilized a conventional molecular dynamics simulation with a pre-assigned neutral solvent charge. Our analysis indicates that solvent polarization influences both the interface's counterion distribution and potential profile. Although the solvent model varies significantly between the two scenarios, this impact has minimal effect on counterion distribution, which remains consistent for high ionic concentrations (a non-depletion scenario). For low ionic concentrations (a depletion scenario), however, solvent polarization results in noticeable changes, pushing counterions away from the interface and thus, adjusting the potential profile. These findings are further confirmed using an analytical approach that utilizes the Poisson-Boltzmann equation.

Our approach seeks to automatically infer executable software specifications from diverse text sources. These specifications comprise key elements such as software purpose, constituent programs, relevant libraries, execution environment, input/output interfaces, and internal components. Our methodology derives these specifications from non-structured texts through a multi-step process involving three main steps: (1) categorizing and reassessing text segments based on significance, (2) utilizing a knowledge graph to incorporate missing software components, and ( inferred specifications from text-based analysis. Our methodology differs significantly from prior knowledge-graph-based approaches as it initially filters and categorizes text segments before integrating knowledge from external sources. To accomplish this, we developed a system that categorizes text segments into software specification-related and general types before assigning weights to each segment in line with the categorization process. Following segmentation, we utilize graph-based algorithms to incorporate knowledge from external sources, resulting in an annotated knowledge graph that guides the construction of inferred specifications.

In a wireless communication network with mobile relay nodes, we examine the energy consumption within a collaborative encoding framework. We develop an optimization model to minimize the energy consumption of relay nodes while adhering to a maximum encoding time constraint. A time limit is imposed on each relay node, and we aim to allocate time intervals along with the optimal power allocation to achieve this goal. Due to the intricate interplay between time interval lengths and power allocation, our problem is classified as a time-fractional quadratic problem. To tackle this complexity, we utilize a specific property of convex quadratic functions and transform the problem into a binary programming problem. Since this problem is NP-hard, we devise a binary search algorithm for joint time interval optimization and a greedy algorithm for power distribution that leverages node-specific characteristics. Our simulation results reveal that the proposed energy-efficient collaborative encoding scheme can substantially decrease the energy consumption of network nodes.

Recent studies of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states in metal adsorbates on superconducting surfaces have shown their existence through the suppression of superconducting properties at impurity sites and surrounding areas. A new theory, based on initial conditions and relativistic principles, has been developed to study the YSR effect in a Mn adatom and Mn dimers on a Nb(110) surface. In this new approach, the spin-down component of the surface superconducting gap was determined using a start value. The calculated in-gap states are in good agreement with experimental data, and the effect of asymmetric YSR states for Mn dimers is observed. The behavior of YSR states in relation to superconducting parameters and local magnetic moments is also investigated.

This research introduces a method that tackles the issue of reducing bias in deep learning based 3D object classification tasks, particularly when it comes to object pose predictions using sequential scan alignment techniques. The proposed approach consists of two main components: a data transformation method that creates modified datasets free from bias by applying processed image transformations, and a method to train a model that uses reconstructed datasets free from bias to correct the predictions made by the primary model.

In this paper, we address the issue of satellite picture edge detection without relying on deep networks, which are often costly to train and difficult to utilize in resource-constrained settings. Our solution comprises two main components: first, we develop a method for selecting significant features from these images, and then, we describe the construction of a traditional edge detection filter. The proposed feature selection method is based on the interpretation of satellite picture edges, with derived features being computationally efficient to compute. The filter itself is built upon the characteristics of edges in these images, with its effectiveness being justified through theoretical analysis. The presented approach has been tested and shown to outperform comparable techniques in handling dark areas and textures, with its performance being further supported by quantitative assessments and visual demonstrations.

In S-XANES data analysis, electron group structure plays a pivotal role.  A newly proposed framework for understanding and measuring the structure of electron groups, based on quantum mechanics, has been developed.  This framework allows the explanation of high-intensity X-ray absorption in terms of transitions involving bound-to-continuum and continuum-to-bound electron groups.  These transitions can be associated with changes in the angular momentum of electron groups and can occur within an atom or between different connected atoms.  X-ray absorption transitions can be classified into four primary categories: (1) the shift of a core electron into a valence group, (2) the reverse transition from a valence group to a core orbital, (3) the simultaneous ionization of core and valence electrons, and (4) the capture of a core electron and emission of a valence electron.  Our framework predicts that these four types of transitions will dominate in S-K and O-K spectra, and can be validated by comparing them with high-resolution photoelectron spectroscopy data, as well as first-principles calculations.  Our framework can also be utilized to analyze and interpret the XANES spectra in materials research.

This paper introduces the concept of imperceptible manipulation in radio frequency signals, a form of cyberattack, and explores its effects on radio signals used for modulation classification. A particular technique, known as image blending, is presented as an example of frequency-dependent manipulation in radio signals. Our investigation examines the characteristics of this form of manipulation and evaluates its impact on commonly used modulation classification deep learning models, including their application in radio frequency signal classification.

Image segmentation in medical analysis is a widely used technique, and when it comes to clinical data, using multiple sclerosis lesions as an example, it often proves to be a highly challenging task. Successful segmentation can significantly impact treatment decisions, and one method to improve this process involves using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) trained on MRI scans. However, implementing these models in real-world clinical settings can be difficult, primarily due to variations in scanning protocols and differences in imaging equipment. To overcome these obstacles, researchers have proposed Continual Lifelong Learning (CLLL) techniques, which enable the model to adapt over time, or alternatively retraining the model from scratch using data from multiple hospitals. In this study, it was demonstrated that incremental learning is a more effective approach than training on aggregated data from multiple hospitals, with specific emphasis on magnetic resonance images and their transferability across different clinics.

We propose "manic contrast" learning as a method to enhance sample efficiency in
contrastive learning. In conventional contrastive models, we optimize embeddings
within a loss landscape shaped like a hyperbolic pair of manifolds, where similar
samples reside in positive wells and dissimilar samples reside in negative wells,
with the distance between them defined by label pairs. In manic contrastive
learning, we perform optimization within an inverted, locally convex version of
these negative wells, referred to as "manic" wells, by inverting the curvature of
the loss landscape, thus producing a mirrored, double-holed, double-humped
geometry. By reversing the optimization direction, we establish a model that
maintains its performance even when queried within the manic wells. Experimental
results on image and sentence pairs indicate that manic contrastive learning outperforms
its traditional counterpart in self-supervised learning benchmarks.

In complex dynamical systems, it's common for models to differ from reality, leading to discrepancies between a system's true behavior and its modeled predictions. These discrepancies can be particularly severe and may result in misleading inferences, rendering them nearly impossible to draw accurately. Model discrepancies can be considered as a form of structural error, and this paper explores the concept of intelligence in handling such errors. Specifically, it examines how an intelligent agent can learn the error patterns in a given model, enabling it to anticipate and predict the system's behavior more accurately. As model discrepancies often exhibit complex and sometimes chaotic dynamics, this paper discusses the development of neural network-based structures to understand and model these errors. In simpler systems, certain theoretical foundations can be applied, but in more intricate systems, additional theoretical frameworks are needed. Consequently, this paper not only outlines potential approaches to creating intelligent systems capable of learning error dynamics but also identifies theoretical gaps and challenges that need to be addressed in order to achieve this goal.

This region contains a high density of dust and gas that is beginning to take shape as a network of clumps and filaments. We have found a significant change in these filaments and observed a core within one of them, called DR-W3, which closely resembles the environment around our own core and nearby star-forming regions. An analysis of how these cores and surrounding line-emitting features move, using a statistical method called moment matching, revealed that DR-W3 core is expanding due to the core next to it, called DR-W5, which moves away at a speed of about 1.5 km/s. Recent findings from Event Horizon Telescope observations have sparked renewed interest in the possibility that dark matter is comprised of small primordial black holes. This concept is being explored through simulated gravitational lensing of magnetic fields in the early universe, which can be computed using the PopSyCLE framework. Our initial experiments, set in primordial conditions, have successfully produced preliminary results, and we are now preparing more comprehensive experiments, including comparisons with recent observational data from Sgr A*.

The concept of a splay variation, where the orientation of individual particles within a system of rigid wedges varies in a radially symmetric manner, is explored in this research. A new phase state is identified within splay variations of basic stages. By using molecular dynamics simulations, equilibrium configurations of systems consisting of hard spheres within a system of rigid wedges were studied. A new phase state, characterized by splay variation of basic stages, was found to occur in systems with splay variations of wedges. This new phase state displays splay variation characteristics and has a splay-free limit consistent with existing findings. Additionally, a new phase state, characterized by splay variations of wedges, was found to occur in systems with splay variations of both wedges and spherical particles. This new phase state displays splay variation characteristics and has a splay-free limit consistent with existing findings. A new phase state, characterized by splay variations of both wedges and spherical particles, was found to occur in systems with splay variations of both wedges and spherical particles. This new phase state displays splay variation characteristics and has a splay-free limit consistent with existing findings.

Our goal is to enhance adaptation capabilities in pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) for diverse downstream tasks, particularly with limited data, while minimizing the number of adjustable parameters. We introduce a novel paradigm called Token Adaptation, which utilizes a single trainable token to adjust VLM parameters for each new task. This approach offers significant advantages, surpassing traditional adaptation methods such as prompt learning and fine-tuning. The Token Adaptation method demonstrates exceptional performance on various public benchmark datasets, including VL-TS, VisText, VL-SC, VL-Bench, and VLBench. Our research indicates that our method outperforms prompt learning and fine-tuning, achieving notable improvements, and represents a substantial step forward in VLM adaptation.

This paper compares two methods of preference-based preference ordering: one that considers all available information and another that considers only preference ratings. The contextual preference model assigns a preference relation to specific data points based on associated contextual information, whereas the non-contextual model assigns a preference relation to entire datasets. The non-contextual model is used to represent preference over datasets with missing data or missing values. The paper demonstrates the non-contextual model's ability to represent strict and weak preferences over datasets with missing data and shows the relationship between the two models. The paper also investigates properties of the induced preference model on datasets when a preference model is given on a domain and investigates how to aggregate contextual preferences to form a non-contextual preference model. The paper specifically investigates whether there are any unrestricted aggregation methods that can produce non-contextual preference from contextual preference components and proves the impossibility of such methods under certain conditions.

Rational Polymer Design, the process of engineering tailored polymers for specific applications, has become a significant area of study in the polymer science community. The ultimate goal is to create polymers with desired properties for various uses, such as enhancing the efficiency of polymer solar cells or developing advanced biomedical materials. The ultimate goal is to move away from trial-and-error methods and instead utilize scientific methods to achieve these goals. The process of designing polymers for specific energy harvesting properties, such as in polymer solar cells, involves careful consideration of how the glass transition temperature of the blend affects the device's energy absorption capacity. The dynamic nature of polymer mixtures and their energy interactions are also key factors in understanding how to design effective polymers for specific energy harvesting applications.

In complex models like transformers, the ability to learn and improve comes from a basic capacity to forget or discard information that is no longer relevant. We refer to this as dynamic rejection processing and it is a crucial factor in shaping how neural networks solve tasks. Our study investigates how the type of transformer model and task influence the development of this processing capability in different transformer models, including those based on pre-trained language models developed by Google and Meta, as well as open-source models like Stanford AI Research's Pre-trained Language Model and State Paper Rejections. We found that the ability to dynamically reject information is strongly linked to the type of transformer model used and the nature of the task at hand. Interestingly, the development of this processing capability tends to be linked to tasks that are linguistically demanding, suggesting a possible connection between its emergence and advanced language skills.

One potential use of machine interpretation is to assist users in generating new content. To develop a more effective interpretation model, it is essential to anticipate the needs of users who are in the process of creating content. In this research, we investigate a text creation process involving human intelligence amplification and identify a key factor - a user's focus - as a critical element. A simple and non-intrusive technique for detecting a user's focus is proposed, and the integration of a user's focus into a machine interpretation model is shown to yield positive results. Our findings are based on a study conducted with actual writers, and the data and interpretation model we developed are now available for others to use and build upon.

Calculations for the Kontsevich value-based contributions of specific graph families, specifically the relation and curvature graphs within the context of symplectic pionners, have been completed. This was done using an alternative framework rooted in the deformation quantization theory rather than formal noncommutative algebra methods, ultimately yielding comprehensive formulas that can be applied universally across n dimensions. These graphs, though not directly contributing to the symplectic star product, are essential in the derivation of Kontsevich's weight formulas for the relevant graph sets.

We've developed a method for determining the critical strength at which a specific interaction within a large-N CFT triggers a phase transition when the theory is heated above a certain temperature. Our investigation involves analyzing the thermal phase diagram of a class of 1+1D Z_N orbifold theories, discovering that the strong-coupling critical strength increases with larger N and at an infinite N, this interaction's thermal phase transition aligns with a point of infinite thermal density matrix rank. Additionally, through examining thermal density matrix purification, we've found that for theories with strong coupling, thermal entanglement remains subdominant to thermal entropy at high temperatures. Furthermore, analyzing large-N couplings reveals that interactions with values below a specific threshold exhibit distinct entanglement properties, including thermal purity and thermal entanglement entropy, indicating that for all large-N interactions, both thermal and entanglement information exhibit distinct characteristics.

Wang and Lin (2021) proposed a valuation framework for Asian options in markets following general Markov processes, suggesting the option value can be broken down into a base option value and a component reflecting the average price's in-money status. However, this research质疑 their derivation of the status indicator, demonstrating inconsistencies in its numerical calculations and presenting alternative approaches for calculating this component, including a stochastic expansion method for even further price process generalizations.

Over recent decades, an unusual phenomenon has been observed in the Cosmic Microwave Background, characterized by correlations across vast distances that cannot be explained by current cosmological models. Similarly, a large-scale gamma-ray background that changes slowly over time suggests the presence of distant, widespread gamma-ray sources. We investigate whether large clusters of galaxies could be the origin of this trend. Utilizing data from the SDSS-III and the Fermi-LAT, we analyze the distribution of clusters and the evolution of their gamma-ray emissions. Our results indicate a correlation between cluster distributions and gamma-ray signals, with clusters located at moderate distances being the most likely source of this trend. Furthermore, our research suggests that a significant portion of the gamma-ray background may be contributed by these clusters, with their collective emissions decreasing over time.

In conventional cosmological collider physics, large-scale structure serves as a probe to investigate the characteristics of the early universe's inflation phase. Non-linear interactions within single field models cause ripples in the cosmic fabric to interact profoundly, potentially exposing the massive particles and signals within to the heavens. Initial oscillations of heavy entities leave behind imprints in primordial temperature fluctuations and subsequent gravitational wave patterns. Our research focuses specifically on intermediate-scale structures formed by the convergence of long-wavelength features and short, oscillating wavelengths, which can act as an indicator for cosmological collider physics.

To better understand how deep convolutional neural networks work for image classification, we propose focusing on a specific, image-dependent set of features in the network's latent space. By incorporating attention mechanisms that adapt to each input image, we developed an ensemble model that refines its internal representations and enhances visual semantics. This approach allows us to gain deeper insights into the network's image classification decisions and assess its robustness to various types of perturbations. Our results, as demonstrated on the MNIST dataset, show that models with attention mechanisms not only achieve higher accuracy but also exhibit greater clarity in their reasoning. Furthermore, we observed that these models exhibit enhanced robustness against adversarial attacks, specifically gradient-based methods.

The electron-phonon interaction, often considered a short-range phenomenon, unexpectedly displays a long-range characteristic when it mediates the interaction between electrons in one-dimensional systems. Notably, when these electrons are arranged in chains with alternating, weakly interacting links, a specific arrangement of charges becomes favorable due to the presence of this long-range, phonon-mediated interaction. Notably, it has been demonstrated that even a relatively small perturbation to these inter-chain connections can cause a phase transition, leading to the emergence of a superconducting state, and for sufficiently strong inter-chain connections, the interaction results in attractive forces between the electrons, thereby facilitating the formation of Cooper pairs and triggering superconductivity.

This study introduces an approach for learning the structural components of dynamic models using self-reported data from individuals. We propose a method that leverages observations of structure and states to learn potential models, allowing for the identification of both dynamic model parameters and network structure. We tested our method using data from the MPHIA dataset, which tracks the state dynamics of drug users. The approach allows for the estimation of potential structures and parameters, and we found that certain parameters are difficult to distinguish due to a high degree of collinearity. We also observed that some states are likely not directly connected, and the estimated structures are consistent with findings from other studies. The potential applications of our method include personalized coaching, risk assessment, and the design of interventions.

The magnetic order of the chiral magnet, specifically the ferromagnetic, A-type antiferromagnetic and B-type antiferromagnetic Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$, is explored in detail. By introducing a liquid helium microjet, the researchers can extract heat at a highly localized point, and in the A-type phase, this leads to the destruction of a skyrmion lattice, which is observed through resistivity and magnetization measurements. This result suggests that the local temperature exceeds the critical temperature for skyrmions. Comparing the results with those of a similar Mn-based material, the researchers can estimate the thermal budget required to destroy the skyrmion lattice and find significant differences between the two materials.

Social networks and other relationships change over time, and the way one entity influences another can shift both in the network's structure and the specific effects within each connection. High-dimensional dynamic influence models are designed to capture these changes over a large number of entities and their relationships. This article provides a comprehensive overview of Selective Sampling Influencing Models, a framework that allows for flexible analysis of these changes. We introduce SIMs to capture three types of influence patterns: linear, non-linear, and non-parametric. We review existing approaches to estimating and analyzing these patterns, as well as considering how to evaluate and measure their effectiveness. A numerical analysis is also conducted to compare the performance of linear and non-linear estimators under varying levels of correlation and dependence. We discuss challenges in selecting appropriate models and parameters for dynamic influence systems, and outline future research directions for improving selection strategies. Finally, we present a select list of open-source software packages used for estimating and modeling SIMs.

This paper introduces an innovative approach to alleviate the imbalance problem in the static point-mesh balance technique. Conventional stiffer matrices employed in static point-mesh balancing tend to result in meshes with extremely small elements, which in turn cause computational errors. We propose a novel energy function specifically designed to prevent infinitesimally small meshes, effectively stiffering small elements without exacerbating larger ones. Consequently, this stiffer matrix yields a more uniform matrix condition number and addresses the inherent stiffer matrix issues. Our experimental outcomes demonstrate significant enhancements over existing static point-mesh balancing methods.

A Bayesian neural network has been introduced as the foundation for creating and retrieving hidden information in images without altering the quality, known as UV-qualitative invisible steganography. By utilizing Bayesian inference, this method offers a reliable solution to the challenge, allowing hidden messages to be both accurately detected and decoded simultaneously. Furthermore, hidden data is only accessible when both the grid's weights and biases are present in the carrier, with model performance demonstrated through experiments using the SPY database.

A key concept in geophysical and astrophysical flows is mean-field dynamo, serving as a theoretical tool to analyze and analyze dynamo processes across the universe, from planetary magnetic fields to the Sun's convective region. However, applying mean-field theory to solar dynamics remains challenging due to the system's complexity. In an effort to address this difficulty, researchers have made significant progress in understanding and modeling the Sun's convective zone, involving numerical simulations, data analysis, and mean-field frameworks. This study aims to contribute to this area by examining the impact of various turbulent influences on mean-field dynamos, with a focus on understanding whether these influences can be reduced to a few essential parameters, such as turbulent Reynolds number and Mach/Alfven Mach number. This study reveals that the complexity of dynamos in turbulent environments requires a comprehensive consideration of multiple turbulent effects, underscoring the need for precise mean-field modeling to accurately predict and understand dynamo processes across the universe.

The galaxy NGC4945, located 10 million light years away, displays signs of heightened star activity in its central area, which is also known as the nucleus of the active black hole. Researchers have identified a massive eruption of gas and dust in the galaxy, which appears to be one of the most significant of its kind in the active black hole's vicinity. Using advanced radio telescope technology, the team captured images revealing a large, rotating cloud of gas and dust in the galaxy, which is spinning at high speed and has a distinct shape resembling a corkscrew. The size of the eruption is approximately 100 times the distance between Earth and the sun, and its velocity is around 1 million miles per hour. Notably, the temperature of the eruption is around 100 degrees Kelvin, indicating that it is primarily composed of molecules such as carbon monoxide and hydrogen cyanide. The findings provide new insights into the complex interactions that occur in the vicinity of active black holes and may help astronomers gain a better understanding of the star activity that takes place in active galaxies.

A novel numerical approach is introduced to solve complex quasilinear diffusion equations that play a significant role in understanding the transport of particles and energy in various plasma and statistical physics systems within finite-dimensional frameworks. Specifically, this method targets highly nonlinear situations where coefficients depend on the local properties of the solution and time. Through extensive numerical experiments, a conservative Galerkin method utilizing quadratic interpolation for local variables demonstrates superior accuracy and stability compared to finite difference and finite element approaches based on global linear reconstructions. Moreover, these results align with theoretical expectations regarding energy conservation, particularly under coarse spatial discretization, enabling effective modeling of turbulent transport in heavily magnetized plasmas with periodic boundary conditions and multiple dimensions.

The recently developed SDIMsym method offers a novel way to solve typical and some atypical equations, including periodic and semi-periodic solutions. A key benefit of a sym method is its ability to maintain the original structure of the solved system, particularly in variable timestep implementations that align with the original system's symmetry when the step size is consistent. Nevertheless, step size doubling techniques typically result in structure damping properties rather than symmetry when using step sizes that are not uniform, which is an issue in typical variable timestep implementations. This paper addresses this specific concern by developing a simple yet effective approach to typical variable timestep SDIMsims for systems of ordinary differential equations, utilizing a midrule that reverses the typical jump rule. The proposed method successfully addresses a specific requirement for a typical variable timestep SDIMsims to replicate continuous symmetry in systems of ordinary differential equations, effectively making it structure preserving in step size doubling. The paper demonstrates this approach by integrating it with the typical Runge-Kutta method to solve typical scalar and vector ODEs for specific problems such as the harmonic oscillator, a double finitely coupled pendulum, a van der Pol oscillator, and additional variable timestep experiments comparing the new method against standard methods for solutions with typical characteristics.

In a Banach space, we have developed conditions for the existence of solutions to the Lyapunov equation in the context of c0-semigroups. We have subsequently established the robustness of the solved Lyapunov equation's solution in relation to perturbed semigroups that also fall within the c0-category. Notably, our approach is more versatile and works with broader classes of semigroups, unlike traditional methods focused on strongly continuous semigroups. This is particularly beneficial as it overcomes difficulties in applying our findings to strongly continuous semigroups, where less restrictive solutions to the Lyapunov equation may lead to unbounded outcomes. We have further illustrated the practical application of our findings through semigroup representations of stochastic systems, such as Feller and difference semigroups.

To aid in the search for the muon (g-2) anomaly, the muon dimuonium state's potential for detecting new physics has been explored. To this end, we introduce MuMuPy, a computational tool that calculates the two-photon exchange between dimuons and different types of matter, including atoms, ions, and molecules. This was achieved by combining and extending theoretical frameworks, specifically by merging and modifying the exchange amplitudes described by both the Breit-Blinn-Tartakovsky and Heberling models. The integration of MuMuPy in experimental investigations is essential for in-depth data analysis and the determination of bound-state corrections.

This paper focuses on the optimal investment and consumption choices of an investor, with the goal of maintaining and possibly improving their wealth relative to that of a more affluent competitor. The less wealthy individual, possessing utility functions based on their total wealth, seeks to maximize a utility function that is heavily influenced by the total amount spent over a particularly long investment period, thereby allowing for computationally efficient solutions to be found. Our theoretical results show the existence and continuity of the value function, which we use in conjunction with numerical methods to solve a challenging Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, using a policy iteration approach.

We are currently undergoing a major shift in our understanding of the Milky Way.
Galaxies like the Milky Way were once primarily viewed as dark, hydrogen gas
reservoirs containing dynamic star-forming regions. However, recent data from
the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer, specifically starlight observations,
have significantly altered this perspective. The prevailing view of the Milky
Way's intergalactic medium has been updated to include gas clouds with higher
extinction rates, which are more tenuous and exhibit signs of motion away from
the galactic disk. These findings are now being applied to other well-known
galactic systems, including the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds. The
interactions between the GMCs and the LMC's surrounding intergalactic gas have
resulted in the creation of a gaseous envelope and leading to tides that affect
both satellite galaxies. The GMC's intergalactic gas has also formed a long
gaseous tail that stretches across nearly 100,000 light years, providing
evidence that these satellites are currently interacting tidally with the LMC.
The Milky Way itself is thought to possess a similar, intergalactic gas
reservoir, and examination of its H I 21 cm emission has revealed a tenuous
intergalactic gas envelope surrounding the galaxy. The presence of this
